case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, in determining intellectual disability under Atkins, a court may (or must) assess the cumulative effect of multiple IQ scores—including their standard errors of measurement—to decide if a defendant has shown significantly subaverage intellectual functioning that renders him ineligible for execution.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Eighth Amendment (as applied in Atkins v. Virginia and subsequent cases governing the constitutional bar on executing individuals with intellectual disability); related federal analogue referenced by amici: 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c) (FDPA prohibition on executing intellectually disabled federal defendants).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Alabama argues that its evidentiary framework gives courts permissible discretion to evaluate multiple IQ scores without being forced into an aggregation methodology that effectively lowers the constitutional threshold. On the petitioner’s view, when a defendant presents several IQ scores clustered in the 70s (e.g., 72–78), courts may treat that body of evidence as indicating the defendant has not shown a likelihood that his true IQ is 70 or below, and federal habeas courts (and the Eleventh Circuit) improperly constrained state-court factfinding by treating multiple above-70 scores as cumulatively supporting an Atkins claim rather than weighing against it.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Smith argues that Atkins (as elaborated by Hall and Moore) requires courts to treat IQ testing as imprecise and to account for the standard error of measurement and clinically accepted practices when evaluating intellectual-functioning evidence. Under that approach, multiple IQ scores should not be treated as rigid cutoffs or simply averaged/stacked against the defendant; instead, courts must consider score ranges, testing conditions, and the full clinical picture, so that a collection of scores in the low-to-mid 70s can still be consistent with an intellectual-disability showing when measurement error and related diagnostic factors are properly considered.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the strongest point: “stacking” multiple low-to-mid-70s scores can, in practice, recreate the very rigidity Hall condemned by turning IQ evidence into a de facto cutoff that sidelines SEM and truncates the Moore clinical inquiry. But as Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Barrett stress, Hall and Moore clearly establish only that States may not treat a score above 70 as “final and conclusive” (or adopt an equivalent categorical presumption), not that the Eighth Amendment prescribes any particular method for aggregating multiple scores on habeas. Under a minimalist approach attentive to institutional legitimacy, I would police only disguised conclusive barriers—leaving States room to weigh multiple tests so long as they genuinely treat each as a range, consider testing conditions, and do not foreclose adaptive-functioning evidence. If the record suggests Alabama’s approach operated as an outcome-determinative presumption, the appropriate disposition is a narrow remand focused on that as-applied question rather than constitutionalizing the Eleventh Circuit’s cumulative-score framework.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Gorsuch’s “de facto cutoff” framing is the strongest point for the Respondent, because a categorical presumption that treats IQ as dispositive could recreate the rigidity condemned in Hall. But that principle, even accepting Hall and Moore at face value, does not supply a clearly established constitutional rule requiring a particular treatment of multiple scores (no stacking, no averaging, no presumption that any overlapping SEM range controls), especially on habeas where we may not extend precedent beyond its holdings. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Atkins left implementation largely to the States, and absent proof that Alabama applied an outcome-determinative rule that foreclosed consideration of SEM, testing conditions, and adaptive functioning, the Eleventh Circuit’s approach amounts to federal supervisory control over ordinary evidentiary weighing. If Alabama truly uses aggregation as a conclusive barrier, that is an as-applied defect under Hall’s logic—not a basis to constitutionalize the Respondent’s preferred multi-score methodology here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch make the strongest point against us: “stacking” multiple 71–75 scores can, in operation, recreate the rigidity Hall condemned by diluting SEM and turning borderline scores into a practical veto. But that concern establishes, at most, an as-applied Hall problem—i.e., whether Alabama has effectively made IQ numbers dispositive despite nominal SEM talk—not a clearly established constitutional requirement (especially on habeas) to use the Eleventh Circuit’s cumulative-score methodology or to treat any SEM overlap with 70 as controlling. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Atkins left States substantial discretion in structuring factfinding, and Hall/Moore target conclusive or outcome-determinative rules that foreclose the clinically informed inquiry, not ordinary evidentiary weighing of several tests alongside adaptive-functioning evidence and testing conditions. Under my methodology, we should police categorical barriers where they exist, but we should not constitutionalize a particular multi-score framework absent a clearer command in our precedents and the Eighth Amendment’s limited, textually untethered doctrine in this area.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh press the strongest point against me: Hall and Moore did not constitutionalize any particular multi-score aggregation method, and habeas limits us to clearly established law. But that framing does not meet the as-applied Eighth Amendment defect Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch identify—an evidentiary approach can be unconstitutional not because it fails to use a mandated formula, but because it functions in practice as a conclusive barrier that discounts SEM and prevents the clinically informed inquiry Atkins, Hall, and Moore require. Justice Alito’s administrability and finality concerns cannot justify a methodology that predictably increases the “unacceptable risk” of executing an intellectually disabled person by turning several low-to-mid-70s scores into a disguised cutoff. So I would hold narrowly that a State may consider multiple scores, but it must treat each as a range and may not let aggregation substitute for, or preempt, the full diagnostic analysis—including adaptive functioning and testing context.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett are right that Hall and Moore did not constitutionalize a particular aggregation formula, and on habeas we should be careful not to turn those cases into a freestanding supervisory regime over evidentiary weighing. But their framing still leaves the key Hall question Justice Sotomayor presses: whether Alabama’s “stacking” methodology, even if not labeled a cutoff, operates as an outcome-determinative presumption that effectively discounts SEM and prevents the full, clinically informed adaptive-functioning inquiry Moore requires. Under a pragmatic textualist approach to our Eighth Amendment precedents, the workable middle is to forbid aggregation practices that function as a de facto cutoff while leaving States leeway to consider multiple scores so long as each is treated as a range and the inquiry proceeds in a clinically coherent way. Justice Kavanaugh’s as-applied characterization is helpful, but if the state court’s method predictably blocks Moore’s holistic inquiry for borderline defendants, that is precisely the “unacceptable risk” Hall held unconstitutional, and it is clearly established at that level of generality.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh offer the strongest counter: Hall and Moore did not clearly establish any particular multi-score aggregation methodology, and on habeas we must resist converting those cases into roving supervision of state evidentiary weighing. But that framing does not answer the constitutional defect I see under Hall’s “unacceptable risk” principle: a State may not employ an approach that, in operation, makes IQ numbers effectively dispositive by treating multiple 71–75 scores cumulatively as a conclusive barrier while functionally sidelining SEM and short-circuiting Moore’s clinically informed inquiry. Justice Thomas’s originalism objection underscores the limits of our role, yet within our existing Eighth Amendment precedents the narrow rule is simply that States cannot recreate a bright-line cutoff by accumulation; they may consider multiple scores only if each is treated as a range and the court meaningfully proceeds to the full diagnostic analysis. That limited, as-applied constitutional constraint respects Atkins’s allocation to the States while enforcing Hall/Moore’s prohibition on rigid decision rules that systematically exclude borderline defendants.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch make the strongest point: “stacking” several 71–75 scores could, in operation, become a disguised cutoff that recreates Hall’s unconstitutional rigidity and increases Atkins’s “unacceptable risk.” But that concern proves too much on federal habeas unless the state court actually treated above-70 scores as outcome-determinative notwithstanding SEM and testing conditions; Hall and Moore forbid conclusive rules that disregard SEM and foreclose the adaptive-functioning inquiry, not any particular multi-score aggregation method. Chief Justice Roberts’s institutionalist approach is persuasive here: we can police categorical barriers (including de facto ones) without constitutionalizing the Eleventh Circuit’s cumulative-score framework or extending Hall/Moore beyond their holdings under AEDPA. If Alabama’s method functioned as a conclusive presumption in this case, that is an as-applied Hall problem, but it does not justify a broader constitutional mandate about how to weigh multiple scores.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Gorsuch’s best point is that “stacking” multiple 71–75 scores can, in operation, replicate the rigidity Hall condemned by turning imprecise numbers into a de facto cutoff. But even accepting that constitutional risk in principle, Hall and Moore—especially as “clearly established” law on federal habeas—do not supply a specific rule about how multiple scores must be treated in combination, beyond forbidding conclusive barriers that ignore SEM and foreclose the clinically informed inquiry. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh stress, the dispositive question is as-applied: whether Alabama actually used aggregation as an outcome-determinative presumption rather than permissible weighing of multiple tests (as ranges) alongside adaptive-functioning evidence. Absent a clearer showing that the state court adopted a categorical presumption, I would not extend our Eighth Amendment precedents to constitutionalize the respondent’s preferred multi-score methodology.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh are right that Hall and Moore do not constitutionalize a particular multi-score aggregation formula, and that on habeas we must avoid announcing a new, rigid method as “clearly established” law. But their framing understates how an evidentiary practice can violate Hall’s “unacceptable risk” principle even without an explicit bright-line rule: if multiple low-to-mid-70s scores are treated cumulatively as dispositive, without range-based treatment of each score’s SEM and the clinically grounded context Moore demands, the method can function as the very conclusive barrier Hall forbids. Justice Alito’s federalism and administrability concerns do not justify a heuristic that predictably skews the factfinding away from the full diagnostic inquiry in a capital setting where procedure and substance are intertwined. The narrow constitutional rule I would apply is not an averaging mandate, but a requirement that multi-score use cannot operate as a de facto cutoff that prevents completion of the holistic, clinically informed analysis.

John Roberts.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia left to the States substantial discretion to develop procedures for identifying intellectual disability, and Hall v. Florida narrowly held only that a State may not treat a single IQ score above 70 as "final and conclusive" while ignoring the score’s standard error of measurement. Hall and Moore require courts to account for measurement error and to avoid nonclinical, rigid rules, but they do not compel an aggregation methodology for multiple IQ scores or require treating several above-70 scores as cumulatively supporting an Atkins claim. Given the absence of a clear constitutional command and the need for narrow decisionmaking that respects state factfinding and federalism, I would hold Alabama may evaluate multiple IQ scores (with SEM considered) without being constitutionally required to cumulate them in the manner the Eleventh Circuit endorsed.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Eighth Amendment’s text does not speak to IQ tests, standard errors of measurement, or any specific methodology for adjudicating intellectual disability, and Atkins v. Virginia left to the States the task of developing “appropriate ways” to enforce the constitutional bar. Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas properly prevent a State from using a rigid numerical cutoff or manipulating clinical concepts to foreclose consideration of intellectual disability, but they do not constitutionalize a particular aggregation rule requiring courts to treat multiple above-70 scores as cumulatively supporting an Atkins claim. Consistent with federalism and the limited role of this Court, Alabama may permit its courts to weigh multiple IQ scores (and their measurement issues) as evidence bearing on whether the defendant has carried his burden, so long as the State does not adopt a rule that categorically excludes defendants from presenting a clinically informed claim. Accordingly, the Eleventh Circuit erred insofar as it converted Hall/Moore into a mandate that constrains state-court factfinding on how to evaluate multiple scores.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Atkins bars executing the intellectually disabled but leaves to the States substantial discretion to implement workable procedures, and Hall v. Florida forbids only a rigid rule that treats a single score above 70 as conclusively disqualifying when 70 falls within that score’s standard error of measurement. Nothing in Hall or Moore v. Texas requires a court to “aggregate” multiple IQ scores (and their SEMs) in a manner that effectively presumes eligibility whenever some scores, viewed with error bars, touch 70; a State may instead weigh multiple above-70 scores as probative evidence against a finding of significantly subaverage intellectual functioning so long as it does not impose an absolute cutoff. Given the practical consequences for finality and administrability in capital cases, and the absence of any clear constitutional command for a cumulative-score methodology, Alabama’s evidentiary framework should be upheld as consistent with the Eighth Amendment. Federal habeas courts should not convert Hall’s narrow ban on a conclusive cutoff into a broader mandate that constrains state-court factfinding.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Atkins v. Virginia, the Eighth Amendment categorically bars execution of persons with intellectual disability, and Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas require courts to follow clinically informed methods rather than rigid legal rules that heighten the risk of executing the intellectually disabled. Hall specifically rejects treating an IQ score as “final and conclusive” and mandates accounting for the standard error of measurement; that principle applies with equal force to multiple scores because stacking or aggregating above-70 results into a de facto conclusive presumption against disability repeats the same constitutional error—substituting a court-made metric for medical uncertainty and the full clinical picture. Consistent with Moore, courts must consider score ranges, testing conditions, and adaptive functioning evidence, ensuring borderline defendants and other vulnerable individuals are not erroneously deemed eligible for death. Alabama may consider multiple scores as part of the evidentiary mix, but it may not employ an aggregation methodology that effectively narrows Atkins by overriding SEM and clinical judgment in a way that increases the intolerable risk of wrongful execution.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Hall v. Florida holds that a State may not use a rigid IQ cutoff that treats scores above 70 as conclusively disqualifying when 70 falls within the score’s standard error of measurement, and it requires courts to consider the score as a range and then proceed to the rest of the clinical inquiry. Moore v. Texas (2017, 2019) reinforces that Atkins determinations must be guided by current clinical standards and may not be distorted by non-clinical, outcome-driven evidentiary rules. Given that IQ testing is inherently imprecise, a court assessing multiple IQ scores must consider their cumulative evidentiary force in a clinically consistent way—including SEM and testing conditions—rather than “stacking” above-70 scores as a practical substitute for a forbidden bright-line rule. This approach best implements the Eighth Amendment bar recognized in Atkins by ensuring a workable, coherent framework that respects medical diagnostic practice while leaving States room to weigh the total record.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Atkins held the Eighth Amendment forbids executing the intellectually disabled, while leaving States some implementation latitude, but Hall v. Florida rejected rigid IQ cutoffs and required courts to account for the standard error of measurement to avoid an “unacceptable risk” of unconstitutional execution. Moore I and Moore II likewise require that the legal inquiry be informed by the medical community’s diagnostic framework rather than state-created, nonclinical rules that systematically skew the determination. If a State’s approach treats multiple above-70 scores as cumulatively foreclosing eligibility without incorporating each test’s measurement error and the broader clinical context, it effectively reinstates the kind of bright-line barrier Hall forbids. The Constitution does not demand a mechanical averaging rule, but it does require that all IQ scores be evaluated in a manner that meaningfully incorporates SEM and accepted clinical practice, which supports Smith’s position here.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Atkins left to the States “the task of developing appropriate ways to enforce the constitutional restriction,” and Hall and Moore, while requiring courts to account for the standard error of measurement (SEM) and to be guided by the medical community’s diagnostic framework, did not mandate a particular aggregation or cumulative-weighting methodology across multiple IQ scores. Hall v. Florida rejected rigid cutoffs that ignore SEM because they create an “unacceptable risk” of executing an intellectually disabled person, but it did not convert SEM ranges into a rule that multiple above-70 scores must be treated as collectively favoring the defendant. Given federalism and workability concerns in administering Atkins claims, a State may permit its courts to weigh multiple scores (with their SEMs) as part of a holistic factfinding inquiry so long as it does not impose an inflexible rule foreclosing consideration of SEM and adaptive-functioning evidence. On that understanding, Alabama’s framework can be upheld as consistent with Hall, Moore I, and Moore II, while avoiding a judge-made requirement that effectively rewrites the constitutional threshold.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Atkins held that the Eighth Amendment bars executing the intellectually disabled but left States substantial "discretion" to develop procedures for adjudicating those claims. Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas prohibit rigid score cutoffs and require courts to account for the standard error of measurement and be guided by the clinical framework, but they do not mandate any single aggregation method (or a one-low-score rule) for multiple IQ tests. Consistent with that precedent and the Eighth Amendment’s limited procedural prescriptions, a court may consider multiple IQ scores—including their SEM—collectively as part of the overall evidentiary record, so long as it does not treat any single score as dispositive or ignore measurement error. Nothing in the text of the Eighth Amendment or this Court’s cases compels the specific cumulative methodology Smith demands, and federal habeas review should not convert Hall/Moore into a rigid rule that displaces permissible state factfinding.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Atkins bars execution of persons with intellectual disability, and Hall v. Florida holds that treating an IQ score as a fixed cutoff—rather than accounting for the test’s standard error of measurement—creates an “unacceptable risk” of executing someone the Eighth Amendment protects. Hall and Moore v. Texas require courts to evaluate intellectual-functioning evidence in a manner informed by the medical community’s diagnostic framework, which means considering IQ scores as ranges and integrating testing conditions and related clinical evidence rather than mechanically stacking multiple above-70 scores to negate disability. Nothing in those cases forbids a court from considering multiple scores, but the Constitution does require that cumulative consideration not operate as a de facto bright-line rule that discounts SEM and thereby elevates form over reliable assessment. Given the Eighth Amendment’s focus on accuracy and procedural fairness in this context, the State may not treat a cluster of low-to-mid-70s scores as categorically defeating an Atkins claim without a clinically grounded range-based analysis.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Eighth Amendment (as implemented through Atkins) permits courts to assess intellectual disability by considering the cumulative effect of multiple IQ test scores—rather than treating any single score as dispositive—when determining death-penalty eligibility.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Eighth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution (cruel and unusual punishments), as applied in Atkins v. Virginia; and, by federal statutory analogy referenced by the United States, 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c) (Federal Death Penalty Act prohibition on executing intellectually disabled defendants).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Alabama (through Commissioner Hamm) argues that States retain constitutionally permissible discretion to structure evidentiary rules for Atkins determinations, including allowing courts to evaluate a defendant’s intellectual-functioning evidence holistically by looking at multiple IQ scores together; the Eleventh Circuit improperly constrained that discretion and misapplied Supreme Court precedent by allowing Smith’s Atkins claim to proceed despite a cluster of IQ scores (75, 74, 72, 78, 74) that, in Alabama’s view, do not make it likely his true IQ is 70 or below when properly considered in aggregate and in context.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Smith argues that Alabama’s framework (as applied) risks executing intellectually disabled people by turning IQ evidence into an overly rigid gatekeeping device—especially where measurement error and clinical standards require careful interpretation of scores—and that the Eleventh Circuit correctly required a methodology consistent with Atkins and later cases (e.g., Hall/Moore) that reject overly formalistic treatment of IQ numbers and demand alignment with contemporary clinical understanding rather than a state-imposed evidentiary approach that effectively bars meritorious claims.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Gorsuch press the best objection: Atkins leaves implementation to the States and Hall/Moore should not become a federal supervisory code for weighing multiple IQ scores. But Hall’s core holding is functional—States may not use IQ evidence in a way that effectively makes higher scores dispositive when measurement error puts 70 in play—and an aggregation practice can cross that line if it predictably screens out adaptive-functioning evidence at the threshold. Justice Alito’s insistence that reversal is required absent a formal “categorical bar” reads Hall too formally; our precedents police unconstitutional operation, not merely labels, and the narrow affirmance I envision would simply require an individualized, clinically tethered inquiry rather than dictating any one-score rule. Because that route enforces only the outer-bound backstop and preserves state discretion on weighting within those bounds, it best fits judicial minimalism and protects institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s “function over form” concern—that aggregation can operate as de facto gatekeeping—identifies the only constitutionally relevant limit under Hall, but it does not justify the Eleventh Circuit’s move from policing rigid cutoffs to supervising how Alabama weighs a full testing record. As Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan frame it, the Eighth Amendment would effectively constitutionalize “clinically tethered” aggregation mechanics whenever a defendant can argue that higher scores “wash out” SEM; that transforms Atkins’s delegated state implementation into ad hoc federal reweighing without any textual or originalist footing. Moore I/II reinforce only the outer-bound prohibition on nonclinical stereotypes and rigid rules that foreclose the inquiry; they do not empower us to dictate the evidentiary force of multiple valid IQ scores absent a categorical bar. Unless Alabama’s approach is shown to be dispositive in practice notwithstanding SEM—rather than an individualized assessment that considers error and adaptive evidence—the Constitution does not authorize federal courts to intervene.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right to emphasize “function over form,” and I agree an aggregation practice would be unconstitutional if it operated as a de facto cutoff that neutralizes SEM and predictably forecloses the Atkins inquiry. But that functional concern does not justify the Eleventh Circuit’s apparent move from policing rigid gatekeeping (Hall) to prescribing how Alabama must weigh multiple valid scores absent a showing the State treated any combined figure as dispositive or refused to consider clinically relevant evidence. Moore’s insistence on clinical tethering addresses stereotyped or outdated criteria, not a federal constitutional requirement that any single low score—or any score’s confidence interval—automatically triggers full satisfaction of the intellectual-functioning prong. Under Atkins’s delegation, federal courts should intervene only when the State’s method is shown to be rigid in operation; on this record, I do not see that kind of categorical bar.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kavanaugh correctly warn against transforming Hall/Moore into a federal “evidentiary code,” but that overstates what is happening if we focus, as the Chief Justice urges, on function rather than formal weighting rules. Hall already constitutionalized a limited but real constraint: States cannot use IQ evidence in a way that makes higher numbers dispositive by nullifying SEM and thereby foreclosing the clinically required, individualized Atkins inquiry—including meaningful consideration of adaptive functioning—when 70 is in play. Justice Alito’s “holistic” characterization fails where aggregation operates as gatekeeping in practice, increasing the risk of executing an intellectually disabled person, which is precisely the Eighth Amendment harm Hall and Moore target. Read narrowly along Chief Justice Roberts’s framing, affirmance does not prescribe a one-score rule; it simply prevents Alabama from using aggregation as a predictable screen that washes out uncertainty and bars potentially meritorious Atkins claims at the threshold.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Gorsuch are right that Atkins leaves implementation to the States and that Hall/Moore do not create a federal evidentiary code or a one-score rule; that is the strongest objection to affirmance. But Chief Justice Roberts’s “function over form” framing answers that concern: Hall’s holding is violated when a state methodology—whether labeled aggregation or otherwise—predictably makes higher scores dispositive by washing out SEM uncertainty and thereby forecloses the clinically required, individualized inquiry into adaptive functioning. Justice Alito’s insistence on a showing of a categorical bar sets the threshold too high under Hall, which polices unconstitutional operation even when the State claims holistic review; the Eighth Amendment backstop turns on whether the procedure creates an unacceptable risk of executing the intellectually disabled, not whether the State used explicit cutoff language. Read narrowly, the Eleventh Circuit can be sustained as requiring a constitutionally compliant, clinically tethered individualized assessment without dictating how Alabama must “weigh” scores, so I do not see a legal argument that undermines my position.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s functional point seriously: an “aggregation” practice could, in operation, become a de facto cutoff that washes out SEM and forecloses the Atkins inquiry. But that concern identifies the constitutional outer boundary already policed by Hall and Moore—no rigid gatekeeping, no ignoring SEM, no untethered stereotypes—rather than a warrant for federal courts to prescribe how a State must weigh multiple valid administrations absent a showing that the State treated the aggregate as dispositive. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on “predictable” dilution of SEM risks converting our Eighth Amendment backstop into a supervisory evidentiary code, displacing the discretion Atkins expressly left to the States. On this record, as Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Barrett stress, the Eleventh Circuit’s approach looks less like enforcing Hall’s anti-gatekeeping principle and more like reweighing evidence, which I cannot square with the Constitution’s text or our limited role.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s “function over form” point is the strongest on the other side: if Alabama’s aggregation practice predictably makes higher scores dispositive and thereby forecloses the Atkins inquiry when SEM puts 70 in play, Hall would bar it. But I remain unpersuaded that the Eleventh Circuit merely policed that narrow outer bound rather than effectively prescribing how multiple valid scores must be weighed, which risks turning Hall/Moore into a supervisory evidentiary code—precisely the federalism and institutional concerns Justice Gorsuch highlights. Moore I/II (as Justice Sotomayor stresses) reinforces that States may not use nonclinical stereotypes or skewed frameworks, yet it still does not authorize federal reweighing absent a showing of a rigid gatekeeping rule or refusal to engage in individualized consideration. On this record and given Atkins’s delegation, the appropriate course is reversal unless the aggregation methodology is shown to operate as a categorical bar in practice notwithstanding SEM and other clinically relevant evidence.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor are right to press that “aggregation” could, in operation, become a backdoor bright-line rule that replicates Hall by making a higher composite score dispositive despite SEM; that functional concern is the best argument on the other side. But as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Hall and Moore supply an outer-bound backstop against categorical gatekeeping, not a federal constitutional directive about how to weigh multiple valid scores absent a showing the State treated the aggregate as dispositive and foreclosed individualized consideration. Chief Justice Roberts’s narrowing is appealing institutionally, yet on this record it still risks endorsing the Eleventh Circuit’s move from policing rigidity to reweighing evidence, effectively displacing the discretion Atkins left to the States. Without a clearly identified rigid gatekeeping feature in Alabama’s approach—rather than a holistic assessment that accounts for SEM and the full testing record—I would reverse.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point—that Hall/Moore are only an “outer-bounds” backstop and not a federal evidentiary code—does not, to my mind, answer the functional question Chief Justice Roberts identifies: whether Alabama’s aggregation methodology predictably operates as de facto gatekeeping that neutralizes SEM and forecloses meaningful consideration of adaptive functioning. Hall’s prohibition is not limited to an explicit bright-line rule; it reaches procedures that, in operation, make higher scores dispositive despite acknowledged measurement error, thereby creating an unacceptable risk of executing an intellectually disabled person. Justice Alito is right that States retain discretion under Atkins, but that discretion ends where a State’s chosen method systematically screens out potentially meritorious claims at step one rather than permitting an individualized, clinically tethered inquiry. Affirming on Roberts’s narrow framing respects federalism by not prescribing a one-score rule while still enforcing the Eighth Amendment’s substantive protection against procedures that functionally defeat Atkins.

John Roberts.reasoning: Atkins leaves States discretion to develop procedures, but Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas make clear that a State may not use IQ evidence in a way that effectively treats a number as dispositive or disregards the standard error of measurement and prevailing clinical practice. A methodology that aggregates multiple scores to deny relief can be permissible only if it does not become a backdoor bright-line cutoff that bars consideration of other evidence when scores (accounting for SEM) place 70 within the range; Hall specifically rejected rules that foreclose further inquiry when the margin of error encompasses 70. The Eleventh Circuit’s insistence that Alabama’s approach remain consistent with Hall/Moore is a narrow application of our Eighth Amendment precedents and protects institutional legitimacy by adhering to the Court’s established prohibition on rigid IQ gatekeeping. Accordingly, I would affirm permitting Smith’s claim to proceed under a constitutionally compliant framework rather than endorsing Alabama’s aggregation rule as applied here.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Eighth Amendment’s text does not speak to IQ tests or to any judicially mandated method for weighing multiple scores, and Atkins v. Virginia expressly left to the States “the task of developing appropriate ways to enforce” the bar on executing the intellectually disabled. So long as Alabama’s approach does not adopt a rigid cutoff that precludes consideration of measurement error and other relevant evidence, nothing in Atkins compels treating any single IQ score as dispositive rather than assessing the evidence cumulatively. To the extent Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas are read to constitutionalize evolving clinical standards and to displace reasonable state evidentiary rules, that reading departs from Atkins’s delegation and should be clarified or reconsidered consistent with the Constitution’s original public meaning and the States’ retained authority in criminal punishment.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia expressly left to the States “the task of developing appropriate ways to enforce” the Eighth Amendment’s bar on executing the intellectually disabled, and nothing in the Amendment’s text or Atkins requires that any single IQ score be treated as dispositive. Hall v. Florida rejected a rigid, one-score cutoff that foreclosed consideration of the standard error of measurement, but it did not compel courts to ignore other relevant IQ results or prevent a State from evaluating intellectual-functioning evidence in a holistic, cumulative way consistent with clinical practice. Moore v. Texas likewise recognizes state “flexibility” subject to narrow outer limits; considering multiple scores together is not an arbitrary barrier but a practical evidentiary approach that reduces the risk of error in either direction and respects States’ administration of capital sentencing. The Eleventh Circuit’s approach, by effectively jettisoning Alabama’s framework, intrudes on the discretion Atkins preserved and is not demanded by Hall or Moore.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Atkins bars executing individuals with intellectual disability, and Hall v. Florida requires that courts apply an approach informed by contemporary clinical standards, including accounting for IQ’s standard error of measurement and avoiding methodologies that create an “unacceptable risk” of wrongful execution. While States retain discretion to implement Atkins, that discretion is constrained by the Eighth Amendment: Moore I and Moore II make clear that courts cannot adopt state-law evidentiary frameworks that functionally defeat Atkins by privileging nonclinical or overly rigid treatments of IQ evidence. Treating multiple IQ scores “cumulatively” may be permissible only if used as part of a clinically grounded, individualized assessment (alongside adaptive functioning) rather than as a gatekeeping aggregation that dilutes SEM and bars consideration of scores within the relevant range. Because Alabama’s approach as applied risks converting IQ evidence into a formalistic barrier and thereby undermining Atkins’ substantive protection, I would affirm allowing Smith’s claim to proceed.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Atkins leaves States room to craft procedures, but Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas impose an Eighth Amendment backstop: a State may not use IQ evidence in a way that makes a numerical threshold effectively dispositive while ignoring the standard error of measurement and contemporary clinical practice. Allowing courts to aggregate multiple scores to rule out intellectual disability can replicate the same constitutional flaw as a rigid cutoff if it functions as a gatekeeping device that forecloses consideration of adaptive functioning whenever some scores exceed 70 despite measurement error. Consistent with Hall and Moore, courts may consider multiple IQ scores, but only as part of an individualized, clinically informed inquiry that does not treat a cluster of scores as conclusively barring an Atkins claim. The Eleventh Circuit’s approach is therefore permissible to the extent it prevents Alabama’s framework (as applied) from operating as a de facto numerical bar to protection the Eighth Amendment guarantees.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia held that the Eighth Amendment bars executing the intellectually disabled but expressly left “to the States the task of developing appropriate ways to enforce the constitutional restriction,” declining to impose definitive procedural or substantive rules. Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas establish outer limits: a State may not adopt a rigid, outcome-determinative IQ rule (like a strict 70 cutoff that ignores the standard error of measurement) or employ nonclinical criteria, but they do not require that any single IQ score be treated as dispositive in the defendant’s favor. Permitting courts to consider multiple IQ scores cumulatively—so long as the State’s approach remains tethered to accepted clinical concepts (including measurement error) and does not function as an inflexible bar—falls within the discretion Atkins reserves to the States and respects federalism and separation-of-powers limits on judicially invented evidentiary mandates. On that understanding, the Eighth Amendment permits Alabama’s holistic assessment, and the Eleventh Circuit erred insofar as it effectively displaced the State’s evidentiary framework rather than policing only the Hall/Moore “outer bounds.”

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia left the primary responsibility to the States to develop workable procedures for identifying intellectual disability, and we should be cautious about converting our Eighth Amendment cases into a rigid, judge-made evidentiary code. Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas prohibit a single-score, bright-line cutoff that ignores the standard error of measurement and contemporary clinical practice, but they do not require treating any one IQ score as dispositive in the opposite direction or forbid courts from considering multiple scores together as part of a holistic assessment. A cumulative approach that accounts for measurement error and permits consideration of adaptive-functioning evidence can be consistent with Atkins/Hall/Moore while preserving administrable state procedures and respecting precedent and federalism. The Eleventh Circuit’s approach appears to unduly constrain that permissible discretion by effectively dictating how states must weigh multiple IQ scores rather than ensuring only that no rigid cutoff bars potentially meritorious claims.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia leaves to the States the task of developing procedures for identifying intellectual disability, and nothing in the Eighth Amendment’s text or Atkins requires courts to treat any single IQ score as dispositive rather than evaluating the evidentiary record as a whole. Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas prohibit a rigid rule that treats an IQ score above 70 as conclusively disqualifying by ignoring the standard error of measurement, but they do not forbid a holistic approach that considers multiple scores cumulatively so long as the methodology remains consistent with clinical principles (including SEM) and does not impose a bright-line bar. Alabama’s approach—assessing multiple test results together as part of an overall intellectual-functioning determination—fits within the discretion Atkins contemplates and avoids the specific constitutional defect identified in Hall. The federal statutory analogy in 18 U.S.C. § 3596(c) likewise supports a categorical bar on execution of the intellectually disabled, not a mandate that any single test control the outcome.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Eighth Amendment rule announced in Atkins bars executing people with intellectual disability, and Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas (2017/2019) require courts to evaluate IQ evidence in a manner consistent with contemporary clinical understanding, including accounting for measurement error rather than using rigid numerical mechanisms that risk foreclosing meritorious claims. Allowing a State to treat the “cumulative effect” of multiple scores as a de facto gatekeeping device—effectively making the highest scores dispositive notwithstanding the standard error of measurement—creates an unconstitutional risk of executing an intellectually disabled person, contrary to Hall’s rejection of formalistic IQ cutoffs. Procedural fairness and practical consequences weigh against an evidentiary framework that predictably screens out claims based on how scores are aggregated rather than on whether the defendant can prove intellectual disability under clinically informed criteria. While States retain latitude in implementing Atkins, that discretion ends where methodology becomes inconsistent with the Eighth Amendment as interpreted in Hall and Moore.
